name: Vitamin K eye cream

card.summary: Topical vitamin K marketed for under-eye dark circles said to have a blood-vessel component; the sources reviewed contain no clinical studies of it.
card.aka: Phytonadione eye cream, vitamin K dark circle cream
card.note: No clinical studies found; effect on dark circles is unproven in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Vitamin K eye cream is a cosmetic product applied under the eyes and marketed for dark circles with a vascular or bruise-like component. Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin best known for its role in blood clotting.

No clinical studies of topical vitamin K for dark circles were found in the sources reviewed, so claims about its effect on under-eye darkness remain untested here.
quick.mechanism: Vitamin K is a cofactor for an enzyme that modifies clotting proteins, which is how it supports blood coagulation. Proponents of the cream link that clotting role to reducing blood pooling under the eyes; this link has not been tested in studies found for this entry.
quick.risks: Reference material on vitamin K notes that no toxicity is known from high oral intakes of K1 or K2, while intravenous injection can cause severe reactions. Those findings concern oral and injected forms, not creams. Dark circles have many causes, including anatomy, pigmentation, allergies and thin skin.

lead: Vitamin K eye cream is a topical cosmetic product containing vitamin K, applied under the eyes and marketed for dark circles that are thought to have a vascular component, meaning visible blood vessels or pooled blood beneath thin skin.

Vitamin K is a group of fat-soluble vitamins: K1 (phylloquinone) from plants and K2 (menaquinones) from animal and fermented foods, with a role as a cofactor for the carboxylation of clotting factors [2].

Periorbital dark circles are attributed to several causes including anatomy, allergies and eye rubbing, medications, thin skin and increased pigmentation [1]. No clinical studies of topical vitamin K for this condition were found in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Dark circles with a vascular component

paras: Reference text on periorbital dark circles lists multiple possible contributors, including bone structure, thin lower-eyelid skin that makes underlying vessels visible, allergic congestion, melanin excess, sleep loss and ageing changes [1]. Treatments named there include vitamin C, caffeine, hydroquinone, lasers, fillers and fat grafting; vitamin K cream is not mentioned in that article [1].

Vitamin K works as a cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which modifies clotting factors so that they can bind calcium [2]. That clotting role is the basis on which the topical product is marketed for bruise-like discoloration, though the reference articles consulted do not address topical use for dark circles [1][2].

Reference text notes that no toxicity is linked to high oral doses of vitamins K1 and K2, and that intravenous K1 can cause severe reactions in rare cases [2]. People taking warfarin are advised to keep vitamin K intake consistent [2]. These statements concern oral and injected vitamin K and have not been shown to apply to creams.
